# nself deploy

<!-- BEGIN PROSE:summary -->
> Deploy the stack to a target environment (local, staging, production).
<!-- END PROSE:summary -->

## Synopsis

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED:synopsis -->
<!-- GENERATED BY tools/wikigen — DO NOT HAND EDIT -->
```
nself deploy [target] [flags]
```
<!-- END GENERATED:synopsis -->

## Description

<!-- BEGIN PROSE:description -->
`nself deploy` builds your stack and deploys it to a target environment using a per-service
sequenced rolling restart. It chains `nself build` then restarts services in dependency order,
waiting for each service to pass a health check before restarting the next.

The restart order is **resolved at deploy time from the project's own compose file**
(`docker compose config --services`), never from a fixed guess list — a project's actual
service names vary (e.g. object storage is always named `minio`, never `storage`; there is no
literal `plugins` service). See [Rolling Restart, Service Order and Downtime](#rolling-restart-service-order-and-downtime).

The target environment can be supplied as a positional argument or via `--env`. The flag takes
priority when both are given. A target is `local` or any environment in the deploy inventory:
every environment in `.nself/control-plane.yaml`, or every `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_<ENV>` variable
(so `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_QA` makes `qa` a target). `staging` and `prod` keep working with no
inventory, and `production` is an alias of `prod` unless the inventory has an environment named
`production`. Only the named environment is deployed or probed; an unknown name is refused with
`E483` and the list of known environments, and the deploy never falls back to another one.

When `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_STAGING` or `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_PROD` is set, the CLI rsyncs the compose
file and env to the remote host, pulls updated images, then runs the rolling restart via SSH.
With no host configured for a remote environment the deploy is refused (`E483`); use `nself deploy local` to deploy on this machine.

When `.nself/control-plane.yaml` is present (or `--server` is passed), `nself deploy` routes
through the topology-aware pipeline (`controlplane.Run`). The pipeline reads each server's
role and SSH capability, skips `read-only` and `hidden` servers automatically, and returns a
non-zero exit code if the primary app server was skipped. Without that file and without
`--server`, behavior is byte-identical to the legacy single-host path.

Targets accept both short and long forms:

| Target | Accepts | Description |
|---|---|---|
| local | `local` | Build and rolling-restart on this machine |
| staging | `staging` | Staging environment (uses `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_STAGING` if set) |
| prod | `prod`, `production` | Production (uses `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_PROD` if set; requires `--force` or `--dry-run`) |
| any other name | the environment's name, e.g. `qa` | An environment from the inventory (uses `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_<ENV>` on the single-host path); loads `.env`, `.env.<name>`, `.env.secrets` (the same list `nself build` uses), never `.env.dev` or `.env.prod`, and a deploy to any remote host never reads `.env.local` (your personal override stays on your machine; `nself deploy local` still loads it) |

An environment named `prod` or `production` is production-class and requires `--force` (or
`--yes`) unless you pass `--dry-run`. The check runs before every deploy path, including the
blue/green canary path. Releases before this change deployed every environment in the
inventory whenever a `.nself/control-plane.yaml` existed, whatever target you named.

A deploy to a remote environment with no host (no inventory entry and no `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_<ENV>`)
is refused with `E483` before anything is built; it never deploys on the current machine. The
blue/green canary flags apply to `local` only; with a remote environment they are refused. In the
control-plane pipeline, a server whose deploy fails makes the command exit non-zero and lists it.
With a `.nself/control-plane.yaml`, a remote deploy first runs the same remote build (no `.env.local`) and writes the validated env snapshot, then ships both the compose file and `.env.<env>` to every server; if the build or snapshot fails nothing is probed or sent. A prod-class environment always uses the `prod` env cascade and is written to `.env.prod` on the host. The env file pushed to the host is read with the same dotenv reader as the build, so both see the same values. An inventory with two environment names that differ only by case is refused, here and in `nself deploy environments`. 
## Access targets and ops profile

`nself deploy access grant`, `revoke`, and `list` accept `--env`, `--tier`, and
`--server`. The selectors may be combined and resolve the matching inventory
hosts in environment, role, and server order. `--host` remains available for an
explicit single host and cannot be combined with a selector. A selector that
matches no hosts is refused before SSH runs. `--dry-run` on grant or revoke
shows each host's resulting change without writing any host. In v1.5 mode,
changes to a prod-tier host require `--yes` or terminal confirmation; an
unconfirmed noninteractive command exits 4 (`E403`). Revoking the last key
still requires `--force` on each host. Selector list JSON has one result object
per host, with its `env`, `server`, `host`, `entries`, and `foreign_count`.
Explicit `--host --json` keeps its existing JSON array.

`nself deploy --profile ops` builds the ops compose profile and defaults to
environment `ops`. An explicit target or `--env` overrides that default.
`NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_OPS` supplies a single-host target when no inventory file
is present. `OPS_DEPLOY_HOST` remains a v1.5 fallback with a deprecation
warning. In v1.5, `nself deploy ops` and `nself ops deploy` use the same
pipeline path as `nself deploy --profile ops`. `--dry-run` prints the profile,
target environment, host, and remote path before any build or SSH action.

### Environment promotion (v1.5)

`nself deploy promote <source> <target> --yes` promotes between inventory environments.
Tiers must move forward or stay equal: `local`, `local-servers`, then `prod`.
Source and target must differ. A prod-tier target requires `--yes` or terminal
confirmation; an unconfirmed noninteractive promotion exits 4 (`E403`).

`--dry-run` prints the ordered plan without contacting or changing a host. With
`--json`, it emits one v1 envelope containing the result and planned steps.
The steps are resolve, confirm, verify, preflight, source-health, capture, build,
compare, snapshot, save, apply, migrate, health, and record. Builds use the target
cascade in a scratch directory. Production values never enter the operator's tree.

Compare proves per-platform image digest equality before taking a snapshot or
changing the target. It resolves every staged compose fragment with the target's
environment files and captures the source using its compose manifest. Each service's
`platform` override selects its manifest; a source platform mismatch is drift.
`linux/arm64/v8` and `linux/arm64` select the same platform. Other variants,
including `linux/arm/v6` and `linux/arm/v7`, remain distinct.
Drift exits 1 (`E490`) and names the affected services and lookup failures.
Services with a compose `build:` context are unverifiable: prod refuses them;
other tiers warn. The snapshot is created, located by tag, and verified before
save or apply. A failed verification exits with `E206` without applying anything.
After apply, running image identities are inspected again before migration. A
changed tag fails promotion and restores files without restoring the database.

Failures after the verified snapshot restore the saved artifacts. The database
is restored only if migration started, followed by another health check.
Successful rollback exits 2 (`E488`) naming the failed step. Failed rollback
stops immediately with `E489`, the snapshot tag, backup ID, and a manual restore
command. The local `.nself/state/promote.json` records each host's saved tar and
changed or absent files. `nself deploy rollback <target>` and the v1.5
`nself promote rollback` shim restore that record when it is the latest change,
using the verified backup on its recorded target host.
Before a promotion database restore starts, recovery persists `db_restore_started`;
after success it persists `DBRestoredAt`. If completion cannot be saved or the
process stops, a retry refuses with `E489`, naming the backup and warning that
the restore may already have run. Verify the database on the backup host first.
If the restore completed (including a restore performed by hand), run
`nself deploy rollback <target> --db-restore-done` to record completion and finish
recovery without restoring again. The flag asserts operator verification; it
does not run a database restore.

Record rollback reapplies all saved stacks before restoring the database, only
when migration started and the backup has not already been restored. An already
rolled-back record changes nothing. The project deploy operation lock covers record
reload, file reapply, database restore, health, and persistence. For `deploy rollback`,
foreign or superseded promotion records use the v1.5 deploy record; an unusable
same-target record is refused with `E485` before remote writes.
Supersession uses the deployment identity saved by the promotion, rather than
timestamp order. On platforms without operation-lock support, rollback follows
the deploy guard's unlocked fallback. If `promote.json` is corrupt, the `E485`
message names the file and tells you to move it aside; `deploy rollback <target>`
then uses `deploy.json`.
Promotions also update the record used by `deploy status` and the next deployment.

With no arguments, `deploy promote` keeps the existing canary flip. In v1.4,
its arguments retain their previous behavior and `promote` keeps its legacy
implementation. In v1.5, `promote <source> <target>` and
`deploy promote-env <source> <target>` delegate to the environment promotion
runner with one deprecation warning per process.

## Progress stream (`--stream`)

`nself deploy <env> --json --stream` and `nself deploy promote <source> <target> --json --stream` print one JSON envelope per line (NDJSON) while the run goes on. An agent can follow a long deploy without parsing text.

- `--stream` needs `--json`. Without it the command exits 1 with `E401` and does nothing.
- `deploy promote --stream` needs both `<source>` and `<target>` (v1.5). With no arguments (the canary flip) it exits 1 with `E401`.
- stdout holds only envelopes. Human progress and any error text go to stderr.
- `--json` without `--stream` is unchanged: one document, as before.
- The exit status is the one the run has without `--stream`. A promote that rolled back exits 2 (`E488`).

Every line is a compact v1 envelope. A progress line has `data.type` `progress` and these keys, all always present (`null` when unknown): `seq` (1, 2, 3, ...), `step`, `phase` (`start`, `done`, `failed`, `skipped` or `rollback`), `env`, `server`, `elapsed_ms` (since the stream began) and `detail`. The schema is `schemas/deploy-progress.v1.schema.json`.

The last line is always a result line, also when the run failed: `data.type` `result`, `data.result` (`ok`, `failed`, `rolled_back` or `rollback_failed`) and `data.steps` (each step with its last status).

```text
$ nself deploy staging --json --stream --dry-run
{"schema_version":"1","command":"deploy","data":{"type":"progress","seq":1,"step":"Deploy staging-app","phase":"skipped","env":"staging","server":"staging-app","elapsed_ms":2,"detail":"dry-run: capability manage"}}
{"schema_version":"1","command":"deploy","data":{"type":"result","result":"ok","steps":[{"step":"Deploy staging-app","status":"planned"}]}}
```

The registry marks the `--stream` flag `output: stream`, so MCP and HTTP keep the single-document form of `deploy`.

## Deploy Strategies

| Strategy | Status | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `rolling` | **Default (v1.1.1)** | Per-service sequenced restart with health-gating. Each service waits up to 60s for `service_healthy` before the next restarts. |
| `blue-green / canary` | **Available via `--canary N` (Y17)** | Zero-downtime: green containers run alongside blue, Nginx shifts N% traffic to green during soak, then promotes to 100%. Requires `NSELF_FEATURE_BLUE_GREEN_DEPLOY=true`. |
| `preview` | Not yet implemented | Falls back to rolling with an explicit warning. |

The `--strategy=blue-green` and `--strategy=canary` flags still fall back to rolling for backwards
compatibility with existing scripts. Use `--canary N` to activate the implemented blue/green path.

See [[cmd-deploy]] for the full per-strategy behavior spec and downtime expectations.

## Blue/Green Canary Deploy (Y17)

Enable with `NSELF_FEATURE_BLUE_GREEN_DEPLOY=true` (feature flag `blue_green_deploy` via `nself flag list`).

### How it works

```
1. Pull new images tagged as green
2. Start green containers (docker compose -p nself-green up -d)
3. Health check green (30s timeout)
4. Nginx upstream: route N% to green (via upstream weights)
5. Canary soak period (default 5 min)
   - Monitor error rate from green containers
   - If error_rate > NSELF_CANARY_ERROR_THRESHOLD (default 1%) → auto-rollback
6. Promote Nginx upstream to 100% green
7. Health check green at 100%
8. Stop and remove blue containers
9. Green becomes blue for the next deploy
```

### Port assignment

| Color | Port offset | Example (Hasura) |
|---|---|---|
| Blue | 0 (base ports) | 8080 |
| Green | +100 | 8180 |

### Examples

```bash
# Canary at 10% (requires NSELF_FEATURE_BLUE_GREEN_DEPLOY=true)
nself deploy local --canary 10

# Canary at 25%
nself deploy staging --canary 25 --force

# Skip canary — flip directly to 100% green
nself deploy local --skip-canary

# Promote a canary to 100% after manual review
nself deploy promote

# Rollback to blue in < 5 seconds
nself deploy rollback local
```

### Backward-incompatible migrations

If a pending migration is not safe to run during canary (DROP COLUMN, DROP TABLE, RENAME COLUMN,
ALTER COLUMN TYPE, NOT NULL without DEFAULT), the deploy is blocked:

```
ERROR: Migration 0042_drop_column_old_name.sql is not backward-compatible.
Run with --force-migration to apply (disables canary, full downtime deploy).
```

Use `--force-migration` to proceed with a full downtime deploy.

### State file

Blue/green state is persisted to `.nself/bluegreen/state.json`. Run `nself deploy status --blue-green`
to inspect the current active environment and canary traffic split.

## Rolling Restart, Service Order and Downtime

The rolling strategy restarts services in dependency order, one `docker compose up -d --no-deps
<service>` at a time, and gates each service before the next one starts. If a service fails its
gate, the deploy halts, names the service, and restarts nothing after it.

**Manifest and env files.** Every compose call uses the same inputs as `nself restart`: all files
listed in `.nself/compose-files.txt` (the base file, plugin fragments, the user override) as `-f`,
and the env files `.env` then `.nself/compose.env` as `--env-file` (later wins). Plugin services
therefore get the variables `nself build` computed for them. The root `.env` is no longer a
fallback for plugin variables: a plugin variable must be in `.nself/compose.env` (run `nself build`).

**Health gate by service kind.** The kind comes from the resolved config (`docker compose config
--format json` over the manifest):

| Service kind | Waits for | Limit | On failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Declares a healthcheck | `healthy` | 60s | E251 (health check timeout), service named |
| One-shot (`restart: "no"`, no healthcheck) | a new run that exits 0 | 60s | non-zero exit fails at once with E250; never exiting, or never starting again, is E251 |
| Anything else | `running`, seen as the same run on two polls 2s apart | 30s | E251, service named |

The rows apply top to bottom: a service with `restart: "no"` and a healthcheck is long-running, so it
waits for `healthy`. For every kind, a container that exited non-zero or is restarting fails the
deploy at once with E250 when a poll sees it. After the last service, every gated service is read once
more, and the deploy fails with E250 naming any that restarted, is restarting, or exited non-zero since its
gate passed. That catches a crash loop that stays up for a few seconds, but it is not a guarantee: a crash
after that final re-check is not detected, and the health checks (`nself doctor`) that follow the roll are
the only backstop. A service with no `restart` line that exited 0 counts as a finished run (Docker's
default policy is "no"), so it is done. Containers left behind by `docker compose run` are ignored: they are not replicas of the
service. A service that appears in the restart order but not in the resolved config fails the deploy
with E252, checked for every service before the first restart. If Docker cannot be read (daemon down, `compose ps` fails), the
deploy stops with Docker's own message and no service code, because nothing is known about the
service; an interrupt (ctrl-c) stops the same way.

**What a failed deploy leaves behind.** Nothing rolls back. Services before the failed one already run
the new config. The failed service is in whatever state `up` left it (running but not ready, restarting,
or exited). Services after it are not touched and keep running the old config. Fix the cause and run
`nself deploy` again: it restarts every service in order.

Init containers that run once and exit never report `healthy`; the old gate waited for that and
aborted real deploys.

**The order is derived from the project's own resolved compose file, not a fixed list.** Before
each restart, `nself deploy` runs `docker compose config --services` over the manifest (locally, or over SSH for a
remote push target) to get the set of services that actually exist, then orders them:

1. **Core services first**, in dependency order, but only the ones actually present:
   `postgres` → `hasura` → `auth`.
2. **Every other present service next**, in the order docker reported them (e.g. `minio`,
   `nginx`, `redis`, `mailpit`, `ping-api`, `auth-server`, `nself-admin` — whatever this
   project's compose actually defines).
3. **Plugin-contributed services last** — any service a plugin fragment in the compose manifest
   adds (and the base file does not define) restarts after everything else.

A service name is never invented. Restarting a name that doesn't exist in this project's
compose (the old fixed order included `storage` and `plugins`, neither of which is a real
compose service name — object storage is always `minio`) used to abort the deploy with
`no such service: storage` *after* earlier services had already been recreated, leaving the
stack half-restarted. This is why the order can no longer be hardcoded.

Example for a project whose compose defines `postgres hasura auth auth-server mailpit minio
ping-api nginx redis nself-admin` (no `storage`, no `plugins`):

| Service | Restart order | Expected downtime |
|---|---|---|
| postgres | 1st | 5–30s (WAL recovery time) |
| hasura | 2nd | 0–10s (waits for postgres) |
| auth | 3rd | 0–5s |
| auth-server, mailpit, minio, ping-api, nginx, redis, nself-admin | 4th onward, in compose order | 0–5s each |
| *(any installed plugin's service)* | last | 0–5s per plugin |

Total deploy time scales with the number of services actually present (roughly ~15s each).
Total user-visible downtime is lower than the deploy duration because each service continues
serving until its replacement becomes healthy.

`--dry-run` cannot query a live `docker compose config --services` (nothing has been built or
pulled yet), so it prints the resolution rule instead of a concrete list — the real order is
only known once the build for this deploy has run.

Use `--skip-health-check` to bypass the 60s gate for known-slow services like MeiliSearch or
Grafana. Set `HEALTHCHECK_TIMEOUT_<SERVICE>` (e.g. `HEALTHCHECK_TIMEOUT_GRAFANA=120s`) to
extend the per-service timeout.

### Custom service env vars in a dry-run

`--dry-run` also prints, for each declared custom service (`CS_1`..`CS_10`), the full list of
environment variable **names** it will receive: the fixed core set (project identity, Postgres,
Hasura, Auth connection info) plus whatever `CS_N_ENV_PASSTHROUGH` and `CS_N_ENV` add. Values
are never printed. This exists so a plain addition to `.env.prod` doesn't get mistaken for
something a custom service will automatically see — it only reaches the service's container if
that service's `CS_N_ENV_PASSTHROUGH` allowlist names it, or `CS_N_ENV` sets it explicitly. See
[Config: Custom Services](Config-Custom-Services.md) for the full precedence rules.

## Remote Push

Set `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_STAGING` or `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_PROD` to a `user@host:/remote/path`
value to enable remote deployments. The CLI:

1. rsyncs `docker-compose.yml` and `.env.<target>` to the remote
2. Runs `docker compose pull` on the remote to fetch updated images
3. Runs the rolling restart on the remote via SSH

```bash
export NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_STAGING=ubuntu@203.0.113.10:/opt/nself-staging
nself deploy staging
```

SSH key defaults to `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`. Override with `NSELF_DEPLOY_SSH_KEY`.

Agent forwarding is always disabled (`-o ForwardAgent=no`). ssh, scp and rsync get their options as
separate arguments from one builder; no option, key path or remote path is ever parsed by a shell.
Before any process starts, the CLI refuses a key path outside `[a-zA-Z0-9/_.~-]` or starting with
`-`, a remote path with shell metacharacters, a leading `-` or a `..` segment, and any ssh option
holding whitespace or a quote (rsync re-splits its `-e` string on spaces).

**Host keys.** Which policy a deploy uses depends on what it sends:

| Deploy path | v1.4 (default) | v1.5 (`NSELF_V15=1`) |
|---|---|---|
| Secrets push (`.env.<target>` copied with scp) | strict | strict |
| Deploy that ships an env file (inventory deploy, `nself deploy <target>` push) | `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new` (being closed, see below) | strict |
| Compose file only | `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new` | strict |

Strict means the CLI scans the host's live ED25519 key and continues only when that key is already
trusted, either in your `~/.ssh/known_hosts` or in the deploy pin file
`~/.config/nself/deploy_known_hosts`. ssh then runs with `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`. Nothing is
copied before the check. Only ED25519 host keys are scanned: a host that offers only RSA or ECDSA
keys fails the strict check (`host key scan ... returned no ED25519 key`).

Known gap in v1.4 mode: deploys that ship env files still use `accept-new`, and any `accept-new`
connection (a probe, a compose-only deploy) records a first-seen key in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`.
Until that is closed, verify a new host's fingerprint before its first deploy (or pin it with
`--trust-host-key`), or run with `NSELF_V15=1`.

**First contact with a new host.** A strict deploy to a host you have never connected to
fails with `E487` and prints the live fingerprint:

```text
E487 unknown host key SHA256:... for deploy@203.0.113.10; verify it, then run nself env target add <env> <server> --trust-host-key SHA256:...
(or connect once with plain ssh and accept the key into ~/.ssh/known_hosts)
```

Compare the fingerprint with the one your provider shows (console or `ssh-keygen -lf
/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub` on the server), then either pin it with
`--trust-host-key`, or ssh to the host once and accept the key. Before this change the v1.4 secrets push
accepted any key on first contact (`accept-new`).

IP-address hosts are pinned under the alias `nself-<ip>-<port>` (for example
`nself-203.0.113.10-22`) and ssh gets a matching `HostKeyAlias`; hosts on a non-default port use
`nself-<host>-<port>`. A pin file holding a line the CLI did not write (a wildcard,
`@cert-authority` or hashed entry) or with group- or world-writable permissions is refused with
`E487`; fix or remove that line and pin again.

- `nself deploy environments`, list all environments and per-server SSH capabilities (JSON)
- `nself deploy status [--blue-green] [--server <name>]`, report current deploy state; `--server` filters to one server; `--blue-green` adds slot info
- `nself deploy rollback [target]`, roll back the last deployment (see below)
- `nself deploy promote`, flip Nginx to 100% green after a manual canary review
- `nself deploy logs [target] [--server <name>]`, tail Docker logs; `--server` streams logs from a specific server via SSH
- `nself deploy health [target] [--server <name>] [--json]`, run `nself doctor`; `--server` runs doctor over SSH on that server
- `nself deploy check-access` **(deprecated)**, verify `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_*` values resolve — use `nself env target probe` instead
### nself deploy environments
Lists every environment defined in `.nself/control-plane.yaml` (or synthesized from
`NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_<TARGET>` env vars) and the resolved SSH capability of each server.
No key material appears in the output.
```bash
nself deploy environments
```
Output:
```json
{
  "environments": [
    {
      "name": "local",
      "kind": "local",
      "servers": [
        {"name": "local", "role": "app", "capability": "manage"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "staging",
      "kind": "remote",
      "servers": [
        {"name": "staging-app", "role": "app", "capability": "manage"},
        {"name": "staging-lb",  "role": "lb",  "capability": "manage"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "prod",
      "kind": "remote",
      "servers": [
        {"name": "prod-app", "role": "app", "capability": "manage"},
        {"name": "prod-lb",  "role": "lb",  "capability": "read-only", "reason": "ssh: permission denied"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```
Capability values:
The `reason` field appears only when capability is not `manage`.
This command fixes a latent Admin 500 error: the Admin UI calls this endpoint to populate the
server-selector before starting a deploy.
### nself deploy status --server
When `--server <name>` is passed and `.nself/control-plane.yaml` exists, the output includes
a per-server capability section alongside the existing state:
```json
{
  "target": "staging",
  "state": "running",
  "servers": [
    {
      "env": "staging",
      "server": "staging-app",
      "role": "app",
      "capability": "manage",
      "latency_ms": 42
    },
    {
      "env": "staging",
      "server": "staging-lb",
      "role": "lb",
      "capability": "manage",
      "latency_ms": 38
    }
  ]
}
```
### nself deploy logs --server
Streams logs from a specific server over SSH:
```bash
nself deploy logs staging --server staging-app
```
The SSH connection uses `BatchMode=yes -o ForwardAgent=no -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`.
Key material is never logged.
### nself deploy health --server
Runs `nself doctor` on a specific server over SSH and streams the output:
```bash
nself deploy health staging --server staging-app
nself deploy health staging --server staging-app --json
```
With `--json`, the remote `nself doctor --json` is called and the structured output is passed
through to stdout.
### nself deploy check-access (deprecated)
**Deprecated.** Use `nself env target probe` for per-server SSH capability resolution.
`check-access` continues to work for backward compatibility. When `.nself/control-plane.yaml`
is present, it probes all servers and emits a deprecation warning, then outputs:
```json
{
  "servers": [
    {"name": "staging-app", "env": "staging", "role": "app", "capability": "manage", "ok": true},
    {"name": "prod-app",    "env": "prod",    "role": "app", "capability": "manage", "ok": true}
  ],
  "all_ok": true
}
```
Without a `control-plane.yaml`, it falls back to the legacy `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_*` env-var check
with the same JSON schema.
## Remote apply in v1.5 mode (`NSELF_V15=1`)

In v1.5 mode every remote deploy (a control-plane environment, or the single-host
`NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_<TARGET>` path) applies a full artifact set instead of pushing one compose
file. v1.4 mode keeps the push described above, byte for byte. One flow runs per environment:

1. **Target snapshot (read-only).** Over ssh, plain file reads on the primary server: the
   plugins installed in its plugin dir (`PLUGIN_DIR` or `NSELF_PLUGIN_DIR` from `<remote_path>/.env`,
   else `~/.nself/plugins`; name, version and `.disabled` markers) and the certificate dirs under
   `<remote_path>/ssl/certificates` (which of `fullchain.pem`, `privkey.pem`, `chain.pem` exist; the
   files are never opened). `nself` is never run on the target. If the local enabled plugin set or
   a version differs, the deploy stops with `E485` (`target drift`) naming each difference, before
   anything is written. Every other server of the environment is read again just before its apply
   and must match the primary.
2. **Scratch build.** The project is copied to `.nself/deploy-build/<env>/` (rebuilt every deploy,
   without `.nself/`, `.git`, `node_modules`, `ssl/`, `backups/`, `.volumes/`, `logs/` and the old
   `docker-compose.yml`). A stub `ssl/certificates/<dir>/*.pem` tree mirrors the target's names, so
   generated cert paths are the target's. `nself build` runs there with the target env cascade. Your
   own project tree is not written to; the stub files are never shipped. The copy leaves out
   `nginx/` files that carry the build marker (`# Generated by nself build`): they are stale
   generated output and the build writes what it owns. Only the nginx files this build generated,
   plus the unmarked files you name in `NSELF_DEPLOY_NGINX_INCLUDE`, are shipped. Every other file
   of your `nginx/` tree is still copied (the build may read it) but not shipped, and the deploy
   output lists it before anything is sent: `[not shipped] nginx/<path> (not generated by this
   build; add it to NSELF_DEPLOY_NGINX_INCLUDE to ship it)`. A marked file of yours that the build
   did not write again is listed as `[not shipped] nginx/<path> (stale generated output this build
   did not regenerate)`. A dry run (`--dry-run`) stops before the scratch build, so it does not
   stage and does not print these lines; they appear in a real deploy.
3. **Path map.** Every absolute local path in `.nself/compose-files.txt`,
   `.nself/compose-env-files.txt`, the merged compose files and the env files becomes the remote
   layout: the project root is `<remote_path>`, plugin fragments live in
   `<remote_path>/.nself/plugins/<slug>/`. A shipped file that still names a local root (scratch
   project, your project, the local plugin dir or your home) fails the deploy before anything is sent.
4. **Deploy lock and pre-deploy backup tar (every tier).** The host takes
   `<remote_path>/.nself/deploy.lock` (an atomic `mkdir`; its `holder` file names pid, host, user,
   time and id). A second deploy or rollback finds it and refuses, naming the holder. If the holder
   process is gone, remove the lock by hand: `rm <remote_path>/.nself/deploy.lock/holder && rmdir
   <remote_path>/.nself/deploy.lock`. Then, before any sync,
   `<remote_path>/.nself/backups/pre-deploy-<id>.tar.gz` (mode 600: it holds env files) takes the
   compose files, env files, plugin fragments, `nginx/` (not `conf.d*/`, except the
   `nginx/conf.d/<name>.conf` files this deploy ships, which the tar also holds when the host has
   them) and `hasura/` that exist, and `pre-deploy-<id>.absent` lists the artifact paths the host
   did not have yet (a created `conf.d/default.conf` included, so a rollback removes it).
   After a fully successful apply only the newest 5 pre-deploy tars plus this deploy's own are kept;
   older ones are removed, one `[pruned] <name> (old pre-deploy tar)` line each. A failed deploy
   prunes nothing, and a prune error is only a warning. Both paths are
   recorded in `.nself/state/deploy.json` (`pre_deploy_tars`, one per host; `pre_deploy_tar` for the
   primary).
5. **Verified backup (tier prod).** Right after the tar and before anything is synced or any compose
   command runs: `nself backup create --tag pre-deploy-<id>` on the host, the backup is found in
   `nself backup list --format json`, and `nself backup verify <id>` must exit 0. Any failure is
   `E206` and nothing is applied. The id is recorded as `backup_id`, the host as `backup_host`. The
   host needs `nself` on the ssh `PATH`.
6. **Artifact sync, in place.** `rsync -a` with no `--delete`: manifests, merged compose files,
   fragments, env files (`--chmod=F600`, mode 600 asserted afterwards), `nginx/` and `hasura/`.
   The project `.env` is the host's own file and is never overwritten: it stays in the compose
   `--env-file` list, and the sync only creates it (empty, mode 600) when the host has none. The
   host keeps `.nself/deploy-shipped.txt`, the list of what nSelf shipped. Before the sync the host
   removes only files that list names, the new set drops, and that carry the `generated by nself`
   marker. A marker-carrying conf nSelf never shipped here (another project's), an unmarked file or
   anything under `conf.d*/` stays. The generated `nginx/conf.d/<name>.conf` files (today
   `default.conf`) ship, and only that one directory: never `conf.d-<env>/`, never a nested path, and
   a conf.d file is never pruned. The host decides, from the file alone: a file at that path whose
   first 5 lines have none starting exactly with `# Generated by nself build` (case-sensitive; a
   hand-written file, or another nself writer's such as `# Generated by nself ssl add`), or that is
   a symlink, is kept and not overwritten: `[kept] nginx/conf.d/<name>.conf (hand-written on the
   host; not overwritten)`. A `default.conf` that is absent on the host is also kept out when any
   other file under `nginx/conf.d*/` or `nginx/sites/` already declares a `default_server`: `[kept]
   nginx/conf.d/default.conf (the host already declares a default_server in <file>; not shipped)`.
   Neither case fails the deploy.
7. **`nginx -t`.** In a throwaway `docker run --rm` container made from the compose `nginx`
   service's image (the lock-pinned image when the stack is locked), with that service's new bind
   mounts read-only at the same container paths. The container is not on the stack network, so every
   compose service name, `container_name` and network alias is added as a host entry (127.0.0.1):
   `proxy_pass http://hasura:8080` passes as it does inside the stack. A failure stops the deploy
   before any reload or start. A stack without an nginx service prints one skip line.
8. **Pull, then recreate preview.** `docker compose pull`, then `docker compose ... up -d --dry-run`
   on the host lists the services it would recreate or create, so a moved tag that recreates a
   service shows up. A service is stateful when it has a volume or a bind mount under
   `<remote_path>/.volumes`. On a production-class target (tier `prod`), a stateful service in the
   recreate set needs `--yes` (or a typed `yes` on a terminal); otherwise the deploy stops with
   `E403` naming the services and nothing is applied. A dry-run line about a recreate or create that
   cannot be parsed or names no known service also stops a production-class deploy with `E403`
   (`--yes` does not cover it); elsewhere it is a warning.
9. **Apply.** Each service in `docker compose config --services` order:
   `up -d --no-deps -- <service>` and the health gate (healthcheck: healthy within 60 s; one-shot:
   exit 0; otherwise running within 30 s and the same run a poll later). `E250` means the service
   is broken, `E251` that it was too slow. After the last service every gated service is read once
   more, a running nginx is reloaded (`nginx -s reload`, only after the throwaway `nginx -t` passed),
   and the host runs the same `nself db hasura metadata apply` as the v1.4 push (strict on staging
   and production-class targets, a warning elsewhere; `NSELF_HASURA_METADATA_STRICT` overrides).

**Limit: build contexts.** The artifact set does not ship build contexts. Before anything is
written, a service with a `build:` context that is not already a directory on the host stops the
deploy with `E485` (`build context not shippable`) naming the services. Publish an image for the
service, or place its context on the host.

**Limits.**

- Only generated `nginx/conf.d/<name>.conf` files ship from `conf.d` (see step 6); `conf.d-<env>/`,
  nested paths and unmarked files never do. `api-docs.conf` is a site conf under `nginx/sites`.
- A `remote_path` that is not directly under a directory named like `NGINX_FRONTED_BY` is refused
  with `E485` (see "Projects fronted by another stack's nginx" below).
- A deploy refused at `E403` (unconfirmed stateful recreate) is restored, but the images the pull
  fetched stay on the host.
- A symlinked directory under the project dir is followed only when its real path is inside the
  real `remote_path`. A link that resolves outside it (for example `nginx/` pointing at a shared dir
  next to the project, or a symlinked `.env.prod`) stops the deploy with `E485` (`symlink outside
  remote_path`) before the lock, the tar and any sync. Move the shared dir inside the project dir.
  A link that stays inside is written through, and the deploy prints a `[notice]` line with the real
  path. The sync never changes the mode of a directory that already exists.
- A `nginx/` file the set ships is never overwritten when it already exists on the host without the
  nself generated marker, the last recorded deploy did not ship it and the host's own
  `.nself/deploy-shipped.txt` does not list it: the deploy stops with `E485`
  (`unmarked file would be overwritten`) before the lock, naming the path. A first deploy onto a
  host with hand-written nginx files stops at the first collision; move or delete the file, then
  deploy again.
- The sync runs one rsync per destination directory over bare file names, so no directory entry is
  transferred and it works with any rsync as sender or receiver. Proven operator-side rsync versions:
  Apple's 2.6.9-compatible rsync (CI on macOS 14, also openrsync) and 3.x (the Linux sim). A Windows
  operator's compose files may hold `C:\...` paths; the path map rewrites them (any separator
  spelling, drive letters case-insensitive) and refuses a leftover.
- Remote steps are non-interactive (`BatchMode=yes`, `ConnectTimeout=10`): use ssh-agent or an
  unencrypted deploy key. A password or passphrase prompt would hang a step that runs in its own
  process group.
- The prune (generated files the new set dropped) is driven by the last recorded deploy in
  `.nself/state/deploy.json`; the host's `deploy-shipped.txt` can only narrow it. With no record
  nothing is pruned.

If any step from the sync to the preview fails, no container has been touched yet. The files this
deploy shipped are put back from the pre-deploy tar in place, the ones it created are removed, and
the host is left as it was. Which paths those are comes from this process (and, for a rollback, from
`deploy.json`), never from files read back from the host; the host's own `.env` and anything the
deploy did not ship are never restored or removed. Directories that already exist keep their mode
and owner. A failure after the first `up` keeps the new files and the error names the tar and
`nself deploy rollback <target>`. A deploy that was refused or restored cleanly leaves
`.nself/state/deploy.json` byte for byte as it was.

**Ctrl-C.** SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP (a closed terminal or ssh session) during a v1.5 apply or rollback cancel the step in flight (ssh and
rsync run in their own process group, so the terminal does not kill them behind the tool's back).
The step in flight is not killed: it gets up to two minutes to finish, so its remote script is not
still running when the restore starts. A second signal while the restore runs prints one line saying so and does not kill it. Ctrl-C at the
`Type yes` prompt aborts the command at once. Before the first `up`, the tar is then restored (on a fresh context, at most 5 minutes) and the
deploy lock is released; after the first `up` the new files stay and the error names the rollback.
This is tested with real signals sent to the apply and to the rollback. SIGKILL, a lost connection or a powered-off
laptop are not covered: the lock stays, and the error for the next deploy says how to remove it.

For v1.5 environment promotion, Ctrl-C cancels the current step and runs compensation
on a fresh context, returning `E488` when recovery succeeds. A provisional
`.nself/state/promote-attempt.json` keeps snapshot and pre-sync tar evidence until
a host keeps changes, when it atomically becomes the `promote.json` authority.
A failed attempt with no changed hosts preserves the previous live promotion.
Interrupted records can be recovered with `deploy rollback
<target>`; the database is restored only if migration started and it has not already
been restored. If the final record write fails after health succeeds, `E489` says
the promotion is live and names the snapshot, backup and pre-deploy tars. It leaves
the provisional record available and does not undo the healthy promotion.

Record rollback checks each recorded remote path, backup tar location, and the
host's applied compose manifest identity before changing any host. A changed path
or artifact identity refuses with `E485`. Restoring a production-class database
requires `deploy rollback <target> --yes` or terminal confirmation; without either,
non-interactive use returns `E403` (exit 4). The `promote rollback --yes` shim uses
the same confirmation rule in v1.5.
Recovery checkpoints completed file and database restores. After a transient DB
restore failure, retry accepts the restored prior manifest (including absence)
and skips file restoration. An interrupted apply without matching tar evidence
refuses with `E485` and names the verified backup for operator recovery.

All ssh and rsync commands use the strict host-key policy; an unknown key is `E487`.

### Projects fronted by another stack's nginx (`NGINX_FRONTED_BY`)

A project that sets `NGINX_FRONTED_BY=<stack>` has no nginx service of its own. The host layout is
`<dir>/<stack>/<project>`: `remote_path` sits directly under the fronting stack's directory (the
front root, `path.Dir(remote_path)`). The build writes the per-service `nginx/sites/*.conf` there,
and the v1.5 deploy ships them as a second artifact root with the same guards as the project root.

- **Target snapshot.** Besides the project's own `ssl/certificates`, the snapshot lists the front
  root's `ssl/certificates` (directory names and which PEM files exist, never a key), and the scratch
  build's stub ssl tree for the fronting stack mirrors it. The apply checks it did not change.
- **Container rule (before the lock).** The deploy finds the fronting nginx by compose labels:
  exactly one running container with `com.docker.compose.service=nginx` whose
  `com.docker.compose.project.working_dir` is the front root (as given or its real path). Zero or
  several is `E485`, naming every running nginx-service container with its working_dir label and the
  fix; nothing is sent. The container must bind-mount `<front>/nginx` or `<front>/nginx/sites`
  (else `E485`). The container ID is kept, never a guessed name, and the deploy only runs
  `docker exec <id> nginx -t` and `docker exec <id> nginx -s reload`: nothing on the fronting stack
  is restarted or recreated, and its `.env`, compose files and `ssl/` are never read, archived,
  copied or removed. The container is re-checked running before `nginx -t`, before the reload and
  before the rollback reload.
- **Guards (before the lock).** The real front root must be the parent of the real `remote_path`.
  The deploy looks only at `nginx`, `nginx/sites` and the `nginx/sites/<name>.conf` paths it ships
  or may prune: a front file that is a symlink (dangling or not) is `E485`, `nginx` as a symlink is
  `E485`, and `nginx/sites` may be a symlink only to a directory under the real `<front>/nginx`, one
  that the container's bind mount covers. Generated site names have no project prefix (`hasura.conf`, `auth.conf`), so a shipped
  path never replaces a host file that is not this project's: an existing file must carry the
  generated marker (a line among the first 5 that starts with `# Generated by nself build`; a comment
  such as `# hand-written, NOT generated by nself build` is not the marker), else `E485`. A marked
  file is replaced only when its `server_name` set equals the shipped file's (order-insensitive and
  not empty); a path this host's previous deploy shipped (`front_shipped`) is also replaced when the
  set equals the one recorded for it (`front_names`). A recorded path is no pass by itself: if
  another project put its own file there, `E485` names the file and both sets, so a sibling project's site is never overwritten, while a file the
  fronting stack generated earlier for this project can be adopted. The fronting stack's own
  `.nself/deploy-shipped.txt` is never read.
- **Front tar.** Right after the project's tar, `<remote_path>/.nself/backups/pre-deploy-<id>-front.tar.gz`
  holds the shipped front paths that already exist (and the files the previous deploy shipped that
  this one may prune); symlinks are never followed into it. Only `nginx/sites/<name>.conf` paths are
  ever in it.
- **Sync and prune.** Right after the project sync, the front files are copied without `--delete`.
  A front file is pruned only when this host's previous deploy shipped it (`front_shipped` in
  `deploy.json`: files shipped, not files pruned, and never merged across hosts) and it carries the
  strict marker above and still has the `server_name` set recorded for it in `front_names`; otherwise
  it is kept (`[kept] ... (server_name changed since this project shipped it; not pruned)`). A record
  without `front_shipped` or `front_names` prunes nothing. The host files are read again right
  before the first front write (after the tar), because the front root has no lock; a change since
  the first check is `E485` and the pre-touch restore runs, leaving the changed file alone. Another project's
  sites are never touched.
- **Test and reload.** Step 7 runs `docker exec <id> nginx -t` in the live fronting container (it
  tests what will actually be loaded) instead of the throwaway container; step 9 reloads it with
  `nginx -s reload`. A failure before the first `up`, including `nginx -t` or a container that
  stopped, restores both roots in place (changed files back, created files removed) and reloads
  nothing. The front root has no lock of its own (the deploy lock covers `remote_path`): if anything
  else reloads the fronting nginx (another fronted project's deploy, a certificate renew hook)
  between the front sync and a restore, it loads the new files and keeps serving them until the next
  reload. The restore says so; reload the fronting nginx again in that case.
- **Rollback.** `deploy.json` records, per host, `front_tars`, `front_changed`, `front_absent`, `front_shipped` and `front_names`.
  `nself deploy rollback` resolves the container first (same `E485` rules), restores the front
  files in place from the front tar, then runs `nginx -t` and `nginx -s reload` there, even when the
  re-apply of the project failed (the error then says the fronting nginx was reloaded). A record
  without these fields, or with an empty `front_changed`, rolls back as before. With the fronting
  nginx down the rollback stops with `E485` before changing anything: start it, then run the
  rollback again.

### Rollback in v1.5 mode

`nself deploy rollback <target>` reads `.nself/state/deploy.json`. When it holds a `pre_deploy_tar`
for the target, it restores the tar on every host in `pre_deploy_tars` in place: extract to a temp
dir under `.nself/backups/`, `rsync -ac` back only the files the record lists as shipped (no
directory is moved or re-moded, so a bind-mounted `nginx/` keeps its inode), and remove only the
listed files that did not exist before. On `backup_host` it then runs `nself backup restore
<backup_id> --yes` when a verified backup was taken (tier prod), and re-applies the restored compose
set with the same pull, per-service `up`, health gate, `nginx -t`, nginx reload and hasura metadata
apply. The database restore returns the data to the moment of the backup: writes made since then,
while the new containers ran, are lost.

The database is restored at most once per record: `db_restored_at` is saved right after
`nself backup restore` succeeds, before the re-apply, so a retry of a rollback that failed later
(on any host) skips it and redoes only files and services. The `backup_host` is rolled back first. If it
kept no changes of the deploy (so it has no tar), the database is not restored: the rollback prints the
backup id and the manual `nself backup restore <id> --yes` command and keeps `backup_id` in the record.
`backup_id` is recorded only once a server ran `up`. If that command itself fails midway the
marker is not set and a retry runs it again. A record already rolled back is refused. The record's
`success` covers every server of the env, with each server's outcome in `host_outcomes`. Without such
a record the older promote rollback below runs.

## Rollback

`nself deploy rollback` is wired to the last `nself promote` tag. Every `nself promote <src> <target>`
call creates a backup snapshot tagged `pre-promote-<target>-<unix>` and writes a promotion record
to `.nself/promotions/<id>.json`. Rollback reads the most recent record and restores the env,
migration state, and Hasura metadata from that snapshot.

**Rollback does not roll back container images.** If you need an older image, pull it manually
(`docker pull nself/...:v1.0.8`) before running rollback.

```bash
# After a failed or unwanted production promotion:
nself deploy rollback prod
# Finds last pre-promote-prod-* backup tag
# Runs: nself backup restore pre-promote-prod-<ts>
# Prints: Rollback for prod completed — prior promote state restored
```

When no promote history exists:

```
Error: rollback failed: find backup: no promotion records found
Run 'nself promote staging' before a deploy to create a rollback point.
```

When the last promote tag is older than 7 days, rollback prompts for confirmation. A stale rollback
may re-apply migrations that no longer match the current code. Review the diff shown before confirming.

**Requires:** `nself promote` must have run at least once against the target environment to create
a rollback point. On a fresh production host, run `nself promote staging prod` before the first
`nself deploy production` to ensure a rollback baseline exists.

## Health Checks

After each deploy (unless `--skip-health` is set), the CLI calls `nself doctor` and checks the
output. If any service is `unhealthy` or has not started within 60s, the deploy result is `failed`
and the specific service name is reported:

```
  [running] Health checks (calling nself health)
  [failed] Health check failed (service: hasura). Run 'nself doctor --verbose' for details.
```

Use `--skip-health` as a break-glass escape hatch. A visible warning is always emitted when used.

## Output format

When `--json` is set, the command writes a structured result:

```json
{
  "target": "staging",
  "strategy": "rolling",
  "steps": [
    {"name": "Build images", "status": "done"},
    {"name": "Restart postgres", "status": "done"},
    {"name": "Restart hasura", "status": "done"},
    {"name": "Restart auth", "status": "done"},
    {"name": "Restart minio", "status": "done"},
    {"name": "Restart nginx", "status": "done"},
    {"name": "Health checks", "status": "done"}
  ],
  "durationMs": 78234,
  "success": true
}
```

The `"Restart <service>"` step names shown above are an example, not a fixed list — they mirror
whatever this project's own compose file actually defines, per [Rolling Restart, Service Order
and Downtime](#rolling-restart-service-order-and-downtime).

Human output uses the same step vocabulary (`done`, `failed`, `skipped`, `running`, `pending`,
`unhealthy`) inside `[...]` brackets so the Admin UI's deploy API route can parse it without
a separate protocol.

## Environment variables

| Var | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_STAGING` | — | SSH/rsync target for staging: `user@host:/path` |
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_PROD` | — | SSH/rsync target for production: `user@host:/path` |
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST` | — | Generic remote host used when target-specific vars are unset: `user@host:/path` |
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_USER` | — | SSH user for remote deployments (used when host is specified without a user prefix) |
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_KEY_PATH` | `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` | SSH private key path for remote deployments (alias: `NSELF_DEPLOY_SSH_KEY`) |
| `STAGING_DEPLOY_HOST` | — | Fallback alias for `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_STAGING` |
| `PROD_DEPLOY_HOST` | — | Fallback alias for `NSELF_DEPLOY_HOST_PROD` |
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_SSH_KEY` | `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` | SSH key path (superseded by `NSELF_DEPLOY_KEY_PATH`; both accepted) |
| `HEALTHCHECK_TIMEOUT_<SERVICE>` | `60s` | Per-service health-check timeout |
| `NSELF_FEATURE_BLUE_GREEN_DEPLOY` | `false` | Enable blue/green canary path (Y17). Set to `true` to activate. |
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_STRATEGY` | `canary` | Deploy strategy when blue/green is active: `canary`, `blue-green`, `direct` |
| `NSELF_CANARY_PERCENT` | `10` | Initial canary traffic % (used when `--canary` is not passed) |
| `NSELF_CANARY_SOAK_MINUTES` | `5` | Soak duration before auto-promote |
| `NSELF_CANARY_ERROR_THRESHOLD` | `1.0` | Error rate % that triggers auto-rollback |
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_HEALTH_TIMEOUT` | `30` | Seconds to wait for green container health |
| `NSELF_BLUE_PORT_OFFSET` | `0` | Port offset for blue containers |
| `NSELF_GREEN_PORT_OFFSET` | `100` | Port offset for green containers |
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_NGINX_INCLUDE` | — | v1.5 remote deploy: comma-separated globs relative to `nginx/` (`sites/hand.conf,includes/*.conf`; `path.Match` per path segment) naming unmarked nginx files to ship besides the ones the build generated. Read from the target's env cascade. Absolute entries, `..` and anything under `conf.d` are refused. |
| `NSELF_DEPLOY_ENV` | `production` | Deploy target environment set by `nself deploy` after resolving `--env` / positional argument. Values: `local`, `staging`, `production`. Exposed for subprocesses and plugins. |

A remote environment needs a host; with none the deploy is refused (`E483`). Multi-region orchestration is available via the dedicated `nself region` command (`list`, `add`, `status`, `promote`).

## Maintenance Banner

`--maintenance-banner` is deferred to a future release (DEP-07). To show a maintenance page manually,
configure an nginx static page via `nginx/conf.d/`.

## Safety

- Production deploys without `--force` are rejected with a clear message
- Use `--dry-run` first to preview steps on any target
- Agent forwarding is disabled by default for all SSH connections (`ForwardAgent=no`)
- SSH connections use `BatchMode=yes StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`
- SSH keys are never logged or included in command output
- `--rollback` validates the promote tag's env against current code before applying; drift
 causes an explicit error rather than a silent misapply
- Primary-server skip gate: when the topology pipeline detects that the primary app server
 has `read-only` capability and was skipped, the command exits non-zero even if other servers
 succeeded. Use `nself deploy environments` to diagnose capability issues before deploying.
- Inline secrets in `--host` or `--key-ref` flags are rejected with an error

## Examples

<!-- BEGIN PROSE:examples -->
```bash
# Local build + rolling restart (positional form)
nself deploy local

# Local build + rolling restart (flag form)
nself deploy --env local

# List all environments and per-server SSH capabilities
nself deploy environments

# Staging dry-run — shows what would happen without executing
nself deploy staging --dry-run

# Staging dry-run with topology plan (when control-plane.yaml exists)
nself deploy staging --dry-run --server staging-app

# Staging dry-run using --env flag
nself deploy --env staging --dry-run

# Deploy to a single server only
nself deploy staging --server staging-app

# Staging deploy with JSON output
nself deploy staging --json

# Production deploy (rolling)
nself deploy production --force

# Production deploy using --env, skipping the confirmation prompt via --yes
nself deploy --env prod --yes

# Production deploy and stream logs until Ctrl-C
nself deploy --env prod --force --follow

# Production deploy with explicit strategy (blue-green falls back to rolling with warning)
nself deploy production --strategy=blue-green --force

# Roll back to the last promoted state
nself deploy rollback prod

# Per-server status (requires control-plane.yaml)
nself deploy status --server staging-app

# Stream logs from a specific server
nself deploy logs staging --server staging-app

# Run doctor on a specific server
nself deploy health staging --server staging-app --json

# Check SSH access (deprecated — use 'nself env target probe' instead)
nself deploy check-access
```
<!-- END PROSE:examples -->
